if_true
def if_true(
    conditional
):


if_true is for quickly creating conditional expressions. The input is a sympy comparison, such as an inequality, and the output is a \(1\) if that comparison is true or 0 if false. It works by creating a piecewise function. E.g.

BLR = Variable("BLR", "Bank liquidity ratio")
z1 = Variable("z_1","Bank liquidity indicator")

z1 << if_true(BLR > 0.12)

\(\displaystyle z_{1} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for}\: BLR > 0.12 \\0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)




source

lag
def lag(
    x:SFCmodeler.term.Term | sympy.core.expr.Expr | float, n:int=1
)->sympy.core.expr.Expr:
Lag every Term in x by n periods (x can be a Term, expression, or constant).



V = Variable("V","Wealth")
Y = Variable("Y","Income")
C = Variable("C","Consumption")

lag(V - (Y-C))

\(\displaystyle - Y_{-1} + C_{-1} + V_{-1}\)




source

d
def d(
    x
):


d allows for a first difference. With a single Variable, You can use it on either the left or right side of an equation:

d(V) << Y - C

\(\displaystyle V = - C + V_{-1} + Y\)



D = Variable("D","Stock of debt")
NL = Variable("NL","New lending this period")

NL << d(D)

\(\displaystyle NL = - D_{-1} + D\)


It works on more complicated expression too, though must be on the right side:

d(Y - C)

\(\displaystyle - C - Y_{-1} + C_{-1} + Y\)



d(2)

\(\displaystyle 0\)

solve_for(d(V) - (Y - C), V)

ModelResults
def ModelResults(
    results, index:NoneType=None, start_period:str='2000', freq:str='Y', reindex:bool=False, debuglist:bool=False
):


ModelResults is a small wrapper around a standard pandas DataFrame, that just adds some nicer indexing, slicing, and plotting.
You won’t usually create one yourself, and instead an SFCmodel will store one in the .data property:

Variable.default_value = 10

C = Variable("C","Consumption")
T = Variable("T","Taxes")
V = Variable("V","Wealth",100)
Y = Variable("Y","GDP")

alpha1 = Parameter("alpha_1","MPC out of income",0.6)
alpha2 = Parameter("alpha_2","MPC out of wealth",0.4)
G = Parameter("G","Government spending",5)
theta = Parameter("theta","Tax rate",0.2)

model = SFCmodel(
    [
        C << alpha1 * (Y - T) + alpha2 * V(-1),
        Y << C + G,
        T << theta * Y,
        V << V(-1) + Y - T - C
    ]
)

model.solve(5)

title: SFCmodeler
text:
How to use
First declare Parameters (fixed exogenous values), Variables (found endogenously by the solver), and any Random elements, each with a name and optional description and initial_value

Variable.default_value = 10  # This sets a default initial value for Variables

C = Variable("C","Consumption")
T = Variable("T","Taxes")
V = Variable("V","Wealth",100)   # The number 100 overrides the default value declared above
Y = Variable("Y","GDP")

alpha1 = Parameter("alpha_1","MPC out of income",0.6)
alpha2 = Parameter("alpha_2","MPC out of wealth",0.4)
G = Parameter("G","Government spending",5)
theta = Parameter("theta","Tax rate",0.2)

Next define the SFCmodel with a list of equations. Each equation should have one variable on the LHS, then << as the equals sign, then any valid Sympy expression:

model = SFCmodel(
    [
        C << alpha1 * (Y - T) + alpha2 * V(-1),
        Y << C + G,
        T << theta * Y,
        V << V(-1) + Y - T - C
    ]
)

You can automate the generation of some of the equations, using the Sector, Asset, Transaction,BSmatrix, TFmatrix, and RVmatrix classes. See the page on Representations for more details.
Run .solve() to solve one period forward, or specify a number of periods to solve more than one time step:

model.solve(5)

title: Representations
text:
from nbdev.showdoc import show_doc

These are optional, but can be helpful if you’re going to do a lot of manipulations or plotting based on the SFC matrices for your model.
For this page, we’ll work with Godley/Lavoie’s model LP as an example:

Variable.default_value = 0

Bcb = Variable('B_{cb}','Government bills held by the Central Bank')
Bd = Variable('B_d','Demand for government bills')
Bh = Variable('B_h','Government bills held by households')
Bs = Variable('B_s','Government bills supplied by government')
BLd = Variable('BL_d','Demand for government bonds')
BLh = Variable('BL_h','Government bonds held by households')
BLs = Variable('BL_s','Supply of government bonds')
CG = Variable('CG','Capital gains on bonds')
CGe = Variable('CG^e','Expected capital gains on bonds')
C = Variable('C','Consumption')
ERrbl = Variable('ERr_{bl}','Expected rate of return on bonds')
Hd = Variable('H_d','Demand for cash')
Hh = Variable('H_h','Cash held by households')
Hs = Variable('H_s','Cash supplied by the central bank')
Pbl = Variable('p_{bl}','Price of bonds')
Pble = Variable('p_{bl}^e','Expected price of bonds')
Rb = Variable('r_b','Interest rate on government bills')
Rbl = Variable('r_{bl}','Interest rate on government bonds')
T = Variable('T','Taxes')
V = Variable('V','Household wealth')
Ve = Variable('V^e','Expected household wealth')
Y = Variable('Y','Income = GDP')
YDr = Variable('YD_r','Regular disposable income of households')
YDre = Variable('YD_r^e','Expected regular disposable income of households')

Parameter.default_value = 0
alpha1 = Parameter('alpha_1', 'Propensity to consume out of income')
alpha2 = Parameter('alpha)2', 'Propensity to consume out of wealth')
chi = Parameter('chi', 'Weight of conviction in expected bond price')
lambda10 = Parameter('lambda_{10}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda12 = Parameter('lambda_{12}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda13 = Parameter('lambda_{13}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda14 = Parameter('lambda_{14}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda20 = Parameter('lambda_{20}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda22 = Parameter('lambda_{22}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda23 = Parameter('lambda_{23}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda24 = Parameter('lambda_{24}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda30 = Parameter('lambda_{30}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda32 = Parameter('lambda_{32}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda33 = Parameter('lambda_{33}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
lambda34 = Parameter('lambda_{34}', 'Parameter in asset demand function')
theta = Parameter('theta', 'Tax rate')

G = Parameter('G', 'Government goods')
Rbar = Parameter('\\bar{r}_b', 'Exogenously set interest rate on govt bills')
Pblbar = Parameter('\\bar{P}_{bL}', 'Exogenously set price of bonds')

model = SFCmodel(
    [
        Y << C + G,                                  
        YDr << Y - T + Rb(-1)*Bh(-1) + BLh(-1),      
        T << theta *(Y + Rb(-1)*Bh(-1) + BLh(-1)),    
        d(V) << (YDr - C) + CG,                 
        CG << (Pbl - Pbl(-1))*BLh(-1),
        C << alpha1*YDre + alpha2*V(-1),
        Ve << V(-1) + (YDre - C) + CG,
        Hh << V - Bh - Pbl*BLh,
        Hd << Ve - Bd - Pbl*BLd,
        Bd << Ve*lambda20 + Ve*lambda22*Rb - Ve*lambda23*ERrbl - lambda24*YDre,
        BLd << (Ve*lambda30 - Ve*lambda32*Rb  + Ve*lambda33*ERrbl - lambda34*YDre)/Pbl,
        Bh << Bd,
        BLh << BLd,
        d(Bs) << (G + Rb(-1)*Bs(-1) + BLs(-1)) - (T + Rb(-1)*Bcb(-1)) - (BLs - BLs(-1))*Pbl,
        d(Hs) << Bcb - Bcb(-1),
        Bcb << Bs - Bh,
        BLs << BLh,
        ERrbl << Rbl + chi * (Pble - Pbl) / Pbl,
        Rbl << 1./Pbl,
        Pble << Pbl,
        CGe << chi * (Pble - Pbl)*BLh,
        YDre << YDr(-1),
        Rb << Rbar,
        Pbl << Pblbar,
    ],
    redundant_equation = Hs << Hh
)

model[:] = {
      alpha1: 0.8,
      alpha2: 0.2,
      chi: 0.1,
      lambda20: 0.44196,
      lambda22: 1.1,
      lambda23: 1,
      lambda24: 0.03,
      lambda30: 0.3997,
      lambda32: 1,
      lambda33: 1.1,
      lambda34: 0.03,
      theta: 0.1938
}
model[:] = {G: 20,
                 Rbar: 0.03,
                 Pblbar: 20}
model[:] = {V: 95.803,
                 Bh: 37.839,
                 Bs: 57.964,
                 Bcb: 57.964 - 37.839,
                 BLh: 1.892,
                 BLs: 1.892,
                 Hs: 20.125,
                 YDr: 95.803,
                 Rb: 0.03,
                 Pbl: 20}

model.solve(15, redundant_tol=1e-4);






source

Sector
def Sector(
    NW:Term | None=None, name:NoneType=None
):
Represents an economic sector, such as Households or Firms.


Create one Sector for each column in your balance sheet and transactions flow matrices.

Production = Sector()
Government = Sector()
CB = Sector()

They don’t need any information, but you can optionally supply a Net Worth variable if one explicitly exists in the model.

Households = Sector(NW=V)



source

Asset
def Asset(
    supplies:dict[Sector | str, Variable]=None, demands:dict[Sector | str, Variable]=None,
    total_supply:Term | None=None, total_demand:Term | None=None, issuer:Sector | None=None,
    price:Term | sp.Expr | sp.Number | float=1, payout:Callable[[Variable], sp.Expr | Term | sp.Number] | None=None,
    name:NoneType=None
):
Represent an asset, real or financial.


The supplies and demands fields should be dictionaries where the keys are Sectors and the values are the Variables from your model that represent the supply/demand for that asset from that sector. If it’s a financial asset, the issuer should be the sector who the claim is against (the liability or equity share), or None if it’s a real asset.

Money = Asset(
    issuer = CB,
    supplies = {
        Households:Hs
    },
    demands = {
        Households:Hh   
        # Note that this model has Hd which is the demand for money before the period, i.e. not identically eqal to Hs, so shouldn't be used here
    },
)

When there are multiple sectors holding the asset, use "Total" to indicate this variable, as in the examples below.
Also, you can optionally provide a payout function. This function will take in one of the relevant Variables (such as Bd here), and should return an expression that indicates what interest payments it makes.

Bills = Asset(
    issuer = Government,
    demands = {
        Households: Bd,
        CB: Bcb
    },
    supplies = {
        Households:Bh,
    },
    total_supply = Bs,
    payout = lambda var: Rb(-1) * var(-1)  # lagged, since bills pay based on previous period's holdings and rates
)

If an asset has a price, include that in the price field:

Bonds = Asset(
    issuer = Government,
    demands = {
        Households: BLd
    },
    supplies = {
        Households: BLh,
    },
    total_supply = BLs,
    price = Pbl,
    payout = lambda var: var(-1)  # bonds here pay $1 per unit bought last period
)

To quickly check if a variable or sector appears on the supplies or demands for this asset, use in:

Bd in Bills

True



Government in Bills

False




source

Asset.payout_to
def payout_to(
    sector:Sector
)->sp.Expr | Term | sp.Number:
Returns an expression representing the payout to the specified sector, from the payout function. (Checks supplies first, then demands.)



Bills.payout_to(CB)

\(\displaystyle B_{cb,-1} r_{b,-1}\)


And returns 0 if the sector doesn’t hold the asset:

Bonds.payout_to(CB)

\(\displaystyle 0\)




source

Asset.sector_zero_expression
def sector_zero_expression(
    sector:Sector | str
)->sp.Expr | None:
Returns the supply minus demand for a sector, but only if there are variables for both. Use ‘total’ to get total_supply - total_demand



Bills.sector_zero_expression(Households)

\(\displaystyle - B_{d} + B_{h}\)


Use with solve_for to generate equations:

solve_for(Bonds.sector_zero_expression(Households), BLh)

\(\displaystyle BL_{h} = BL_{d}\)




source

Asset.sector_zero_expressions
def sector_zero_expressions()->list[sp.Expr | None]:
Returns list of all sector zero expressions.



Bonds.sector_zero_expressions()

\(\displaystyle \left[ - BL_{d} + BL_{h}, \  - BL_{d} + BL_{s}\right]\)




source

Asset.market_zero_expression
def market_zero_expression(
    demand_or_supply:str='supply'
)->sp.Expr | None:
If demand_or_supply == ‘supply’, returns total_supply minus supply for each sector. If demand_or_supply == ‘demand’ returns total_demand minus demand for each sector. Uses opposite term if none is available for that sector.



Bills.market_zero_expression('supply')

\(\displaystyle - B_{h} - B_{cb} + B_{s}\)


Use with solve_for to create equations:

solve_for(Bills.market_zero_expression(), Bcb)

\(\displaystyle B_{cb} = - B_{h} + B_{s}\)




source

BSmatrix
def BSmatrix(
    sectors:list[Sector], assets:list[Asset]
):
Representation of Balance Sheet matrix, bringing Sectors and Assets together.



bs = BSmatrix(
    sectors = [Households, Production, Government, CB],
    assets = [Money, Bills, Bonds]
)



source

BSmatrix.assets
def assets(
    sector:Sector
)->list[Variable]:
Returns a list of the assets for the specified sector (looks in demands first, then supplies).



bs.assets(Households)

\(\displaystyle \left[ H_{h}, \  B_{d}, \  BL_{d}\right]\)




source

BSmatrix.asset_values
def asset_values(
    sector:Sector
)->list[sp.Expr | Variable]:
Returns a list of the values of the assets (asset times price) for the specified sector. (Looks in demand first, then supplies.)



bs.asset_values(Households)

\(\displaystyle \left[ H_{h}, \  B_{d}, \  BL_{d} p_{bl}\right]\)


Use sum to quickly get the asset side of a sector’s balance sheet:

sum(bs.asset_values(Households))

\(\displaystyle BL_{d} p_{bl} + B_{d} + H_{h}\)




source

BSmatrix.liabilities
def liabilities(
    sector:Sector
)->list[sp.Expr | Variable]:
Returns list of liabilities for the specified sector. First uses ‘Total’ supply, but adds for each sector if that’s not present.



bs.liabilities(Government)

\(\displaystyle \left[ B_{s}, \  BL_{s}\right]\)




source

BSmatrix.liability_values
def liability_values(
    sector:Sector
)->list[sp.Expr | Variable]:
Returns list of the values of the liabilities (asset times price) for the specified sector.



bs.liability_values(Government)

\(\displaystyle \left[ B_{s}, \  BL_{s} p_{bl}\right]\)


Use sum to quickly get the liability side of the balance sheet:

sum(bs.liability_values(Government))

\(\displaystyle BL_{s} p_{bl} + B_{s}\)




source

BSmatrix.net_worth
def net_worth(
    sector:Sector
)->Variable | sp.Expr:
Returns the net worth variable for the sector if there is one, otherwise sums assets minus liabilities.



bs.net_worth(Households)

\(\displaystyle V\)



bs.net_worth(CB)

\(\displaystyle - H_{s} + B_{cb}\)




source

BSmatrix.sector_zero_expression
def sector_zero_expression(
    sector:Sector
)->sp.Expr:
Returns sum of assets minus sum of liabilities minus net worth for a sector. (Note: will return zero if there’s no NW variable defined on the sector.)



bs.sector_zero_expression(Households)

\(\displaystyle - V + BL_{d} p_{bl} + B_{d} + H_{h}\)


This can be useful to use as a key to ModelResults, to check that you get zero, i.e. that the balance sheet balances in your simulation results.

model.data[bs.sector_zero_expression(Households)].plot()








Or use with solve_for to generate equations:

solve_for(bs.sector_zero_expression(Households), Hh)

\(\displaystyle H_{h} = - B_{d} - BL_{d} p_{bl} + V\)


But don’t forget that you will get identically zero if there’s no NW Variable defined in the Sector:

bs.sector_zero_expression(Government)

\(\displaystyle 0\)




source

BSmatrix.sector_zero_expressions
def sector_zero_expressions()->list[sp.Expr]:
Returns a list of zero expressions for all sectors, but only ones with NW variables defined on the sector.



bs.sector_zero_expressions()

\(\displaystyle \left[ - V + BL_{d} p_{bl} + B_{d} + H_{h}\right]\)


Feed this as a key to ModelResults in order to check balance sheet identities for all sectors at once.


source

BSmatrix.asset_zero_expressions
def asset_zero_expressions()->list[sp.Expr]:
Returns asset supply minus demand for all assets in the balance sheet.



bs.asset_zero_expressions()

\(\displaystyle \left[ - H_{h} + H_{s}, \  - B_{d} + B_{h}, \  - BL_{d} + BL_{h}, \  - BL_{d} + BL_{s}\right]\)


Use this as a key to ModelResults to check asset demand/supply consistency for all assets at once in your simulation results:

model.data[bs.asset_zero_expressions()].plot()










source

Transaction
def Transaction(
    entries:dict[Sector, sp.Expr | Term]
):
Represents a row in a Transactions Flow matrix.


Create a Transaction by supplying a dictionary where the keys are Sectors and the values are the expressions for that sector in the transaction:

Consumption = Transaction({Households:-C, Production:C})
GovernmentExpenditures = Transaction({Government:-G,Production:G})
Income = Transaction({Production:-Y, Households:Y})
CBProfits = Transaction({CB:-Rb(-1)*Bcb(-1), Government:Rb(-1)*Bcb(-1)})
Taxes = Transaction({Households:-T, Government:T})

Note that we’ve skipped transactions for interest payments, changes in assets, and capital gains – the matrices below will build these for us. But, let’s create one just for illustrative purposes:

InterestOnBills = Transaction({Households:Rb(-1)*Bh(-1),Government:-Rb(-1)*Bs(-1),CB:Rb(-1)*Bcb(-1)})

Quickly fetch an expression for a sector by indexing:

CBProfits[Government]

\(\displaystyle B_{cb,-1} r_{b,-1}\)


Including uninvolved sectors:

Consumption[CB]

\(\displaystyle 0\)

TFmatrix
def TFmatrix(
    sectors:list[Sector], transactions:list[Transaction], assets:list[Asset] | None=None
):
Class representing the Transactions Flow matrix.



tf = TFmatrix(
    sectors = [Households, Production, Government, CB],
    transactions = [Consumption, GovernmentExpenditures, Income, CBProfits, Taxes],
    assets = [Money, Bills, Bonds]
)

assets is optional, but if you put it in, the matrix will generate additional transactions automatically for interest payments and changes in stocks. Then you can use the matrix to generate expressions or equations as follows.


source

TFmatrix.sector_zero_expression
def sector_zero_expression(
    sector:Sector
)->sp.Expr:
Returns the sume of a column (income - spending - change in holdings) for specified sector.



tf.sector_zero_expression(Government)

\(\displaystyle - G - BL_{s,-1} - B_{s,-1} + \left(- BL_{s,-1} + BL_{s}\right) p_{bl} + B_{cb,-1} r_{b,-1} - B_{s,-1} r_{b,-1} + B_{s} + T\)


Use this with solve_for to generate sector transaction equations:

solve_for(tf.sector_zero_expression(Government),Bs)

\(\displaystyle B_{s} = - T + BL_{s,-1} p_{bl} + B_{s,-1} r_{b,-1} - BL_{s} p_{bl} - B_{cb,-1} r_{b,-1} + G + BL_{s,-1} + B_{s,-1}\)




source

TFmatrix.sector_zero_expressions
def sector_zero_expressions()->list[sp.Expr]:
Returns the sume of a column (income - spending - change in holdings) for all sectors.



tf.sector_zero_expressions()

\(\displaystyle \left[ - B_{d} - C - H_{h} - T + \left(- BL_{d} + BL_{d,-1}\right) p_{bl} + B_{h,-1} r_{b,-1} + BL_{h,-1} + B_{d,-1} + H_{h,-1} + Y, \  - Y + G + C, \  - G - BL_{s,-1} - B_{s,-1} + \left(- BL_{s,-1} + BL_{s}\right) p_{bl} + B_{cb,-1} r_{b,-1} - B_{s,-1} r_{b,-1} + B_{s} + T, \  - B_{cb} - H_{s,-1} + B_{cb,-1} + H_{s}\right]\)




source

TFmatrix.transaction_zero_expressions
def transaction_zero_expressions():
Return all transaction zero expressions (row sums).



tf.transaction_zero_expressions()

\(\displaystyle \left[ - C + C, \  - G + G, \  - Y + Y, \  - B_{cb,-1} r_{b,-1} + B_{cb,-1} r_{b,-1}, \  - T + T, \  0, \  B_{h,-1} r_{b,-1} + B_{cb,-1} r_{b,-1} - B_{s,-1} r_{b,-1}, \  BL_{h,-1} - BL_{s,-1}, \  \left(- H_{h} + H_{h,-1}\right) + \left(- H_{s,-1} + H_{s}\right), \  \left(- B_{d} + B_{d,-1}\right) - \left(- B_{cb,-1} + B_{cb}\right) + \left(- B_{s,-1} + B_{s}\right), \  \left(- BL_{d} + BL_{d,-1}\right) p_{bl} + \left(- BL_{s,-1} + BL_{s}\right) p_{bl}\right]\)

def change_in_sector_holdings(
    sector
):
Sums the change in asset holding entries for a particular sector.



tf.change_in_sector_holdings(Government)

def RVmatrix(
    sectors:list[Sector], assets:list[Asset]

Create a revaluation matrix by specifying the assets and sectors it should contain:

rv = RVmatrix(

rv[(Bonds, Households)]

title: SFCmodel
text:
The SFCmodel class holds the model equations and solver.


source

SFCmodel
def SFCmodel(
    equations:NoneType=None, redundant_equation:NoneType=None, start_period:str='2000', freq:str='Y'
):


First create the terms using Parameter and Variable and Random, and then create a model by writing equations in a list, using << as the equals sign:

Variable.default_value = 10

C = Variable("C","Consumption")
T = Variable("T","Taxes")
V = Variable("V","Wealth",100)
Y = Variable("Y","GDP")

alpha1 = Parameter("alpha_1","MPC out of income",0.6)
alpha2 = Parameter("alpha_2","MPC out of wealth",0.4)
G = Parameter("G","Government spending",5)
theta = Parameter("theta","Tax rate",0.2)


model = SFCmodel(
    [
        C << alpha1 * (Y - T) + alpha2 * V(-1),
        Y << C + G,
        T << theta * Y,
        V << V(-1) + Y - T - C
    ]
)

Optional additional arguments include a redundant equation, and a start and period length for the time index (which defaults to yearly begining with 2000).

model = SFCmodel(
    [
        C << alpha1 * (Y - T) + alpha2 * V(-1),
        Y << C + G,
        T << theta * Y,
        V << V(-1) + Y - T - C
    ],
    redundant_equation = V << V(-1) + G - T,
    start_period="2020",
    freq="Y"  # these are pandas PeriodIndex strings
)

If you have not already set inital_values on the Variables and Parameters, you can set them on the SFCmodel, either one at a time:

model[Y] = 10


model[Y]

\(\displaystyle 10.0\)



model.data[V].iloc[-1].squeeze()

\(\displaystyle 100.0\)


Or as a whole set using “:” and a dict (or anything that will parse to one):

model[:] = {
 C: 10.0,
 G: 5.0,
 T: 10.0,
 V: 100.0,
 V(-1): 100.0,
 Y: 10.0,
 alpha1: 0.6,
 alpha2: 0.4,
 theta: 0.2
}


# This will work too
model[:] = [
 (C, 100.0),
 (G, 50.0),
 (T, 100.0),
 (V, 1000.0),
 (V(-1), 1000.0),
 (Y, 100.0),
 (alpha1, 0.7),
 (alpha2, 0.3),
 (theta, 0.1)
]

Quickly get a text-presentable dataframe overview of what you just set using .inventory():

model.inventory()

The redundant equation refers to the accounting identity that is overdetermined, as typical in SFC models. If you specify it, then the solver will check that it holds (within solver error) every period, and warn you if not. You can also check it manually using .check_redundant_equation:

model.check_redundant_equation()

{'lhs': 100.0, 'rhs': 95.0, 'inside tolerance': False}


In this case the check fails because our default values are not consistent (though that won’t matter for this model, because the equations don’t look back to the values of these variables from previous periods).
.solve() runs the solver for the (optional) specified number of periods, and returns the results

model.solve()   # solves one period
model.solve(3)  # solves 3 more periods

model.check_steady_state(detail=True)

{'converged': [], 'not converged': [C, T, V, Y]}


Instead of specifying a certain number of periods to solve, you can also ask the solver to find the steady state of the model, using the steady argument:

model.solve(100, steady=True);
# The number 100 becomes give_up_steps, with the solver searching for a steady state but stopping after give_up_steps.




Under the hood, the steady state checker calls .check_steady_state, which uses np.isclose to compare the last two timesteps (comparing growth rates for variables declared with growth=True).
Instead of steady=True, you may also pass a dict that can specify a list of variables to ignore:

# rewind the clock:
model.data = model.data[:"2028"]

model.solve(100, steady={'ignore':[C, T]});




You can also include any kwargs to np.isclose in the steady dict (or in arguments to check_steady_state() if you want to call it manually), but specify rol_g and atol_g as rtol and atol for the growth variables.

title: Terms
text:
source


def Term(
    *args, **kwargs
):
A symbolic term in an SFC model.
Terms are thin wrappers around Sympy symbols, mainly to implement lags and equations. There are three kinds, Parameters,Variables, and Random.
source

Parameter
def Parameter(
    *args, **kwargs
):
An exogenous value, not calculated by the solver.
Declare a parameter with its LaTeX name, and an optional description and initial value. Be sure to store it in a variable for later use in an equation.
alpha1 = Parameter("alpha_1","Marginal propensity to consume",0.5)

alpha1

\(\displaystyle \alpha_{1}\)
source

Variable
def Variable(
    *args, **kwargs
):
An endogenous value, solved each timestep.
The interface for a Variable is the same as for a Parameter, defined with a LaTeX name and optional description and initial value:
Y = Variable("Y","GDP",100)

Y

\(\displaystyle Y\)
And you can also optionally set growth=True. This will prompt SFCmodel.check_steady_state() to compare growth rates instead of levels for this variable, so use it if you’re trying to automatically find a steady state:
V = Variable("V",growth=True)
source

Random
def Random(
    *args, **kwargs
):
A random value, generated each timestep.
eps = Random("varepsilon","Expectation error")

eps

\(\displaystyle \varepsilon\)
The default distribution is a standard normal, but you can alternatively supply your own scipy.stats random variable (anything that a .rvs() call will work on) using the distribution argument:
from scipy import stats
phi = Random("varphi","Animal spirits",stats.bernoulli(0.6))

phi

\(\displaystyle \varphi\)
You can set optionally set the seed for the random number generator like this. (Do so before creating any random variables, because the initial value is populated on creation by default, unless you specify an initial_value on the variable on creation or using Random.default_value before creation.)
seed = 42
Random.set_seed(seed)
# alternatively, set Random.generator to a numpy generator

title: Terms
text:
Using terms
Instead of setting default values separately for every term, you can alternatively set them for the whole class, such as:

Parameter.default_value = 0.3
alpha2 = Parameter("alpha_2")

Variable.default_value = 10
G = Variable("G")

Or set them for both Parameters and Variables by using Term:

# Delete the specific defaults if you assigned them, otherwise skip this part
del Parameter.default_value
del Variable.default_value

Term.default_value = 20
gamma = Parameter("gamma")
C = Variable("C")

You can add a lag to a term by putting it in parentheses:

Y(-1)

\(\displaystyle Y_{-1}\)


Then use these in equations like any other symbol.
Create equations using << in place of the equals sign - this is just a shorthand for creating Sympy equations:

C = Variable("C","Consumption")
I = Variable("I","Investment")
Y = Variable("Y","GDP")

Y << C + I

\(\displaystyle Y = C + I\)
